items.title: Forest fire threatens tourist town in Colombian Andes
items.summary: A forest fire was burning Sunday in central Colombia near the popular tourist town of Villa de Leyva, officials said.

items.title: New Zealanders pick endangered black robin as Bird of the Year
items.summary: A record number of New Zealanders turned out at the polls this month, not for national elections but to vote for their Bird of the Year—the critically endangered black robin.

items.title: Indonesia doing 'everything' but still struggling to curb fires
items.summary: Indonesia is doing "everything" to fight huge forest fires, but dozens of planes and thousands of personnel are still struggling to contain them, a senior official said Monday.

items.summary: The stereotype of bland British food is notorious, and people mock the horrors of jellied eels and overcooked vegetables. items.title: 'Rusty treasure' find revealed as Europe's largest assemblage of prehistoric iron bars
items.summary: Analysis of a "rusty treasure" excavated during industrial gravel extraction at Deinham, Austria, reveals it is the largest mass find of prehistoric iron bars in Europe, pointing to iron production and trade during the Iron Age on an unprecedented scale.

items.summary: Stand on the damp sand on a California beach and chances are you're standing on top of an active earthworks site. items.title: How firelight may have shaped the origins of spoken language
items.summary: When asked about the greatest innovation of humans, people often say language or fire. A new paper suggests these innovations may be more interlinked than we previously assumed.

items.title: Venus ate its moon: How Earth's 'twin' could have swallowed a rocky satellite
items.summary: Scientists have long speculated why Venus, with a size, mass and structure similar to Earth's, doesn't have a moon. New UC Riverside research shows that our hungry twin likely swallowed it.

items.title: Virtual cells built from 4D AI models and 'digital twins' could speed up drug discovery
items.summary: Mitochondria—tiny structures that convert nutrients into energy—are often depicted as discrete kidney bean-shaped objects. But in reality, they form a dynamic, interconnected network throughout the entire cell, rapidly splitting and fusing as they're transported to where energy is needed most.

items.title: The story of Little Italy's Feast of San Gennaro is the story of how Italian immigrants became American
items.summary: For two weeks in September, everyone wants to be Italian—at least judging by the crowds at the annual Feast of San Gennaro in New York City's Little Italy.

items.title: Satellites show Earth lost more than 12 trillion tons of ice from Greenland, Antarctica in 47 years
items.summary: About 12.5 trillion tons (11.3 trillion metric tons) of ice from glaciers in Greenland and Antarctica have melted since 1979, which is enough frozen water to stack ice 5 feet (1.5 meters) deep across the continental United States, according to a major scientific report.

items.title: Scientists discover a hidden “ID card” in cat urine
items.summary: Cats may identify one another through a surprisingly durable chemical “calling card” made from 13 unusual fatty acids in their urine. The compounds appear linked to mysterious fat droplets in the kidneys and may represent a scent-recognition system shared across the cat family.

items.title: Scientists may have solved a 2,000-year-old Dead Sea Scrolls mystery

items.title: New nanoparticles make hidden chemical differences light up
items.summary: Scientists have developed ultra-bright nanoparticles that can detect tiny amounts of chemicals and distinguish between molecules that look almost identical. The technology could one day provide a cheaper way to catch dangerous drug impurities or trace pollutants using simple low-cost lasers.
